In the eyes of these moms, "good parents put their children first," Bandelj wrote in her book. "And good parents show how much they love their children by how they spend, save, invest or borrow for them."
Bandelj interviewed 120 parents for her book, and she heard over and over again from moms that "children are at the center of their universe," she said.
None of these words came from dads.
Like many new parents, Rachel Martin took a class at her local hospital in St. Louis, Missouri, before the birth of her son. It touched on how to prepare for labor and feed the baby. But on sleep, she got only a warning: "It's a war zone, good luck."
A class couldn't have adequately prepared her for the fear that seeps in for many parents once the sun begins to set, the baby edition of Russian roulette. Will your baby refuse to sleep, plunging you deeper into a state of insurmountable sleep deprivation — or, totally randomly, sleep for hours?
It's here where the baby marketing industry swoops in most effectively. Parents told The 19th that sleep products felt the most predatory because so much of the marketing banked on people's inexperience and exhaustion.
The products and courses are also some of the most expensive on the market. The Snoo, a robotic bassinet that can detect crying or fussing, soothing babies to sleep with automated rocking and white noise, costs $1,995. You can also rent it, starting at $159 a month. Influencer Cara Dumaplin's Taking Cara Babies course, which promises to teach parents how to train their infants to sleep independently from as early as five months, costs $179. She has 2.8 million Instagram followers.
For some parents, these products and courses improved their postpartum lives.
But Martin felt like she was being bamboozled. So many of the Instagram posts she saw showed tips on each slide, but when she scrolled to the last one there was almost always an upsell: "But for my No. 1 tip, you gotta buy this."
"They have the secrets and I need them — that's what it felt like," Martin said.
Three months into new parenthood, Martin was still getting only a couple of hours of sleep every night. She was willing to consider anything that would help her and her son sleep better.
Martin opted for a $57 course that promised to establish good sleep habits and gradually teach the baby — with minimal crying — to sleep independently. But shortly after she started watching the videos that came with it, she realized she wasn't learning anything she didn't already know. Bedtime routines, red night-lights that won't overstimulate the baby — she knew this from other (free) parenting advice she read. "I was frustrated with myself," said Martin, 34. "I was influenced to spend money on services to not have my baby cry."
She unfollowed the creator, a mom and sleep consultant certified through the Institute of Pediatric Sleep and Parenting, an online accreditor that is not recognized by the U.S. Department of Education.
On Long Island, Sarah Moeller was influenced to buy many items when she had her first daughter, who is now 8. Maybe the most outlandish was a vibrating paddle that slipped under the mattress to lull her baby to sleep. But rather than a gentle rocking, it shook the crib so violently that it tapdanced across her laminate floor.
"Before having children, everybody thinks that they remember or that they know what it's like to be tired," said Moeller, 41. "We all think we know what it is to go without sleep for a little while, but I have not ever experienced something comparable." The algorithm responded to that. In those first months with a newborn, Moeller said she "felt very wronged" by advertising and messages online.
"Sleep deprivation is a form of torture, and I think that really plays into our spending habits," said Dr. Leah Rappaport, a Boston pediatrician who is also a content creator. Rappaport had her children while she and her husband were still in their medical residency, and she found herself buying every major sleep product out there: the Snoo, the Taking Cara Babies course, the swaddles. "I was a pediatrician, and I was absolutely floored by having a child," said Rappaport, 41.
In those first unmooring months, moms are sucked into the online world of algorithms not just because they're desperate, but because they need community.
"You're alone by yourself in the middle of the night with a baby, and there's someone else who is experiencing that," Rappaport said. "And I think that that's where that power is for the product placement."
To get these courses and products in front of expectant parents at just the right time — before their brand loyalties are cemented and when they're more likely to buy impulsively — companies have mined customer data for years.
More than a decade ago, Target started identifying which shoppers may be pregnant by analyzing changes in their spending habits. Target learned that pregnant people were more likely to buy unscented lotions and vitamin supplements in the second trimester. Those insights allowed them to assign a pregnancy prediction score to customers. By 2012, that system was already so advanced that Target could predict a customer's due date window and send coupons and ads to match their stage of pregnancy.
On other sites, any pregnancy data that moms share — like the date of their last period, often put into a due date calculator — can be sold to advertisers. Pregnancy sites like BabyCenter have turned this into something of a science. Moms come for the handy calculator, stay for the newsletter on developmental milestones and the forums, and get their data packaged for the website's sponsors who can then use it to send personalized ads. One of the most popular options for advertisers: slapping ads for baby products onto articles listing baby name ideas, where moms spend more time perusing, historian Lara Freidenfelds found in her book "The Myth of the Perfect Pregnancy."
"In featuring baby name articles so early, BabyCenter is trading on women's excitement, encouraging them to be highly involved and emotionally attached to their pregnancies, and bringing them into contact with a panoply of advertisers at an early stage of pregnancy," she wrote.
Christine Mattheis, the vice president of content and brand solutions at BabyCenter, said the site does collect information from users, including their due dates, "and uses it to deliver stage-tailored content and relevant advertising."
"We disclose our practices transparently in onboarding and our privacy policy, and we provide tools for users to manage their advertising preferences," she said.
However, several of the major baby websites, including BabyCenter, Babylist and The Bump, have been accused of allegedly sharing user data without consent. A lawsuit against Babylist filed last year claims the website allowed third parties including Meta and Google to access user data input during the sign-up process "to help Babylist assist its marketing, advertising, and data analytics efforts." Attorneys are still investigating allegations against Babylist; affected parents who file a claim may be entitled to as much as $10,000.
On social media, creators have gotten more sophisticated about converting viewers to buyers through applications like Manychat. A creator may put something in the caption of a video like, "Comment sleep and I'll send you my top sleep tips!" Manychat runs the back end, and when that comment comes in, the user immediately gets a link in their DMs with the tips, course or products being promoted. The company said it sends billions of these messages a year.
Those sometimes include what are known as "deep links" for, say, Amazon. Clicking those takes prospective buyers not just to the Amazon website but directly to the Amazon app where they're already signed in, making the conversion to a purchase as simple as possible.
The DM links also give brands a channel to contact you — they can follow up with more messages and more items, said Paige Connell, a content creator who specializes in talking about the mental load of motherhood.
Connell said all of this targeted marketing is deeply gendered. Women control about 85 percent of household purchases and for decades have been the object of advertisers' affections. They've been targeted through daytime TV ads, magazines and, now, social media, where content is fed on a continuous loop.
"The second I became pregnant, my Instagram feed became heavily about pregnancy and babies, and my husband's remained about woodworking and golf," Connell said.
No wonder Mom feels like she's on a "perfect mom hamster wheel," she said. "We are marketed to so heavily and then criticized for following through."
In the quest for perfect parenting, it's easy to find yourself drowning under a pile of Amazon boxes. But what we buy our kids actually matters very little.
In the United States, where babies have more access than those in other places to the really important stuff — enough to eat, a stable environment and someone who loves them — parents are already giving their kids just about everything they need to succeed. To give it a number, they're about 95 percent of the way there, Oster said. So it actually doesn't matter which toy subscription box you sign up for (or if you sign up for one at all).
"It's such a funny conversation, because there is a set of people who are obsessively trying to optimize on the last 5 percent, or maybe 2 percent or 1 percent … when there is vast space for improving the lives of kids that has kind of nothing to do with the conversations that we're having over here. That's a real tension in this space. Most of the time, when people ask me, 'How do I do blah optimally?' the answer is, 'It does not matter.'"
Bandelj, the sociologist, lands in a similar place. "This whole idea of, 'We can do all of this for our kids, and then they will be perfect,' that parents influence children the most — that's a prevalent idea, but the research shows it's not that much," she said. We don't have as much control as we think we do, "and it's very hard to hear that."
It wasn't until the newborn fog lifted that FitzGerald started to realize how predatory all the baby product marketing felt. By six months, Rowan was waking only once or twice a night. At 3, he sleeps soundly until the morning. FitzGerald doesn't track sleep anymore with her second son, Ciaran, who is almost 1. She doesn't obsessively scroll in the night. Most of the products Ciaran has are secondhand.
"I have so much grace for her," FitzGerald said of the version of herself who tracked poops and naps in an app.
If she could go back, she would tell her past self that how Rowan slept had nothing to do with her value as a mom. And that she probably didn't need so many swaddles.
"I think I just would tell her, 'You don't have to worry so much,'" she said. "'If Rowan only napped in your arms today, it's not going to ruin him for life. He's a really smart, really thoughtful, really cool kid, and how he slept when he was eight weeks old had no impact to the cool kid he has become.'"
She would try to tell her something that would undo the guilt and shame she felt when her baby acted differently than the others. Something helpful, so that she wouldn't place that blame on herself.
But, actually, thinking back on it now, would she even have believed herself if she'd heard it firsthand? When everything else around her told her she was failing if she didn't buy all the things?
The truth, FitzGerald said with a chuckle, is "absolutely not."

articles.summary:
New parents in the United States are increasingly targeted by a $60 billion baby product industry that leverages social media algorithms to exploit parental exhaustion and insecurities.

### Key Points
- The U.S. baby product market is projected to grow 40% by 2033, driven largely by online sales and premium, tech-focused items.
- Targeted advertising often begins during pregnancy, with companies using data tracking to deliver personalized ads for sleep aids, monitors, and courses.
- Many parents report feeling pressured to purchase expensive items like the $1,995 Snoo bassinet or $179 sleep courses to achieve "perfect" parenting outcomes.
- The lack of federal paid family leave in the U.S. leaves many mothers isolated and sleep-deprived, making them more susceptible to digital marketing promises.
- Several major baby websites, including Babylist, have faced legal scrutiny over allegations of sharing user data with third-party advertisers without consent.

### Why it Matters
The aggressive marketing of baby products capitalizes on the lack of community support and the intense pressure for parents to optimize their children's development. This cycle of consumption often creates unnecessary financial and emotional strain, despite expert consensus that most purchased gadgets have little impact on long-term child outcomes.
